en: The national flower, sampaguita, blooms year-round and releases its strongest fragrance at night to attract pollinating moths.
The Philippine eagle, our national bird, has specialized crest feathers it can raise or lower to communicate in the forest.
During the Pahiyas Festival, locals decorate their houses with colorful kiping, which are leaf-shaped wafers made from ground rice.
The Ifugao people carved stone-walled rice terraces into steep mountains to capture rainwater and prevent soil erosion.
Scientist Ramon Barba discovered that spraying mango trees with potassium nitrate makes them produce flowers even during dry seasons.
The South Sea pearl, our national gem, forms inside oysters when a tiny irritant gets trapped under their shells.
In Bulacan's Carabao Festival, farmers wash their carabaos in the river to thank the animals for helping plow the fields.
T'boli weavers create T'nalak cloth by extracting red and black dyes from the roots and leaves of local abaca plants.
While exiled in Dapitan, hero Jose Rizal built a water system and collected over three hundred specimens of local insects.
The narra, our national tree, drops its small compound leaves during the dry season to conserve water before sprouting new ones.
Marine scientist Angel Alcala proved that protecting coral reefs from dynamite fishing allows colorful fish populations to visibly recover.
Early Filipinos built balangay boats from large hardwood trees like the dungon, using wooden pins instead of metal nails.
